paragraphs: By nightfall the floodwaters had still not drained from Ye’s eastern market. An ox cart carrying millet had sunk into the mud. The driver raised his whip several times but could not bring himself to strike. In the end, two women waiting for porridge called others over. They laid down old door planks and levered the wheel free. Beside the cart, a child chased fallen grains through a puddle. His mother scooped him up from behind and brushed the mud from the back of his hand.
By the time Murong Chui passed, lamps had been lit in the old palace to the northwest.

One of them was a palace lantern he would have known even through a broken wall. In his youth, whenever the ruler of Yan feasted his ministers, lanterns with green gauze shades had hung before Zhaoyang Hall. Gilded bronze trays beneath their frames caught the light and made the jade pendants shine. No one knew whose household had acquired the bronze trays since. Only the gauze shade remained, shivering in the night wind.
Pei Heng handed his reins to a guard outside and accompanied him to a side entrance.
“Everyone inside is an old minister of Yan,” he said. “Will you really take no one with you, General?”
“If I bring men, they won’t speak.”
“And if one of them means to keep you in there forever?”
Murong Chui smiled and touched his waist. It was empty. He had come to supervise flood relief and had left his sword in camp.

“Since you’ve followed me this far, keep watch at the gate. The troops outside the old palace are not to enter first. Anyone who comes out armed or gathers men with blades—deal with him under the standing regulations.”
Pei Heng looked at him without moving aside. “His Highness charged me with overseeing the relief army. Some say I was sent to guard against you.”
“You were. Then do it properly.”

Half a stone balustrade had collapsed inside the palace. Murong Chui stepped over it, gathering mossy mud on his soles. It had once bordered a covered walkway. He remembered a winter when Murong Ke had scolded guards for trampling the new snow beside it, only to nearly slip himself, setting the assembled officers laughing. As Murong Chui crossed the stone, he almost heard that laughter again.

More than a dozen dining mats had been laid in the hall. Under the candles, age spots showed on the hands of old ministers lifting their cups. Some wore the round-collared robes of Qin officials; others had discreetly fastened belts embroidered with ancient Xianbei patterns. One short old man still wore at his waist a bronze cord of former Yan, its seal fitting long since lost.
They rose together when they saw Murong Chui.
“We pay our respects to the Prince of Wu.”
He stood just inside the doorway for a moment.
Han Yin held up a wine vessel. Age had lowered his eyebrows, but not altered his voice. “Does Your Highness still remember this servant?”
“I do. You were a Secretariat gentleman. When you drafted Murong Wei’s confession of fault, you described the offenses of the hundred officials in considerable detail.”

A hint of embarrassment crossed Han Yin’s face, but he still invited him to the place of honor. Behind it hung an old map of Longcheng. The silk had rotted along its edges; the red lines of its city walls remained inappropriately bright.
Murong Chui did not go there. He chose a mat by the door.

“Let us speak first. There are people outside the palace waiting for grain. If this wine is only an invitation to remember old times, we can share a cup and depart. If there is something else, say it before the night grows late.”

The elderly Master Feng, seated beside Han Yin, folded his hands in greeting. He had once taught Murong Chui’s younger brother to read, and his white beard rested on his collar. But the younger Muyu Huan could not restrain himself. “Hebei starves after the flood, the Qin troops sent here all obey the general, and the people call you Prince of Wu when they see you. What is this if not Heaven’s will?”
Murong Chui looked first not at him, but at the millet on the table.
“Where did you buy this?”
“Our households put it together,” Han Yin answered.
“Yesterday, outside the western gate, a peck of millet cost two bronze hairpins. You must have gone to some trouble to provide so much.”
Several men blushed. Han Yin held his ground. “This old servant has lived in Ye for twenty years. Qin is Qin, Yan is Yan. Fortunes turn. What princely house was ever destined to serve forever?”

He ordered a map unrolled. It was not the old chart of Longcheng, but a newly drawn map of Hebei, marked with roads, ferries, granaries, and military camps. The villages inundated by the flood had been swept away in a stroke; the names of former garrison posts were marked in painstaking detail.

“Thirty thousand relief soldiers in Ye. They come from different provinces, but ultimately they answer to your command. The estates still keep household troops. An old veteran in the north needs only a handwritten summons to come.” Han Yin touched the site of the former capital. “Take Ye first and await responses on every side. The man in Chang’an is a thousand leagues away. How could he come to its aid?”
“How many men?” Murong Chui asked.
“A thousand or two of the old troops. Enough for a vanguard.”
“And grain?”
“The government granaries are inside the city.”

Murong Chui turned the map toward the candlelight. “Within three days, the western granary must distribute grain to seven shelters in the southern suburbs. The ever-normal granary is nearly empty. Will you seize the western granary first, or leave its stores for the hungry?”
Muyu Huan burst out, “We can relieve them after Yan is restored!”
“How many days?”
“What?”

“How many days to restore Yan? The bridges are gone, the highways under water. How many days would a battalion take to reach us from Changshan? What will the people outside the walls eat in the meantime?”

Han Yin raised his hand to silence the young man, his expression hardening. “The general has been in Qin too long. Every sentence is about granary stores and land registers. How can a great enterprise under Heaven be calculated down to the last measure of rice?”

“It can,” Murong Chui replied. “Former Yan fell when men like you refused to calculate. The soldiers at Jinyang went all winter without salt while banquets were held every night in Ye Palace. I asked for horse fodder at the front. The dignitaries said the road was too far and I should wait until the following year.”
Master Feng slowly set down his cup. “The court failed you then. This old man knows it. But in these twenty years, has Your Highness never seen your father and brothers in dreams?”
Murong Chui glanced at the map of Longcheng. His fingers rested on the edge of his table and remained still for a long time.
“I have. I have also seen people my own armies failed to reach in time.”
“If Your Highness remembers, why destroy the very roots of Yan with your own hands?”

Murong Chui remembered the rain at Hongnong. A pregnant woman had knelt all afternoon before a granary door, cold water pooled beneath her knees. He had divided his own millet cake and given her half. She accepted it, but asked only, “Will there be any tomorrow?” It was then he realized that for all the power he had once wielded in Hebei, he had no answer to that simple question.
He looked up at Han Yin. “Has Murong Wei sent a letter?”

Han Yin hesitated and produced an unsealed copy. Its language was circumspect: the old servants feared for the realm; the sovereign remembered his ancestors and should know where he stood. There was no original.
“Who delivered it?”
“A former envoy.”
“His name?”
“I cannot say.”
“You wish to use his name, and I wish to know what he actually said. If he had written in his own hand that Hebei must be plunged back into war, why hide the messenger?”
Han Yin did not answer. Someone beside him murmured that the former ruler of Yan was in Chang’an and had to be cautious.
“Then it is you who want to rebel,” Murong Chui said.
A light clatter ran through the feast. Muyu Huan shot to his feet, drawing a short knife from his sleeve. Han Yin rebuked him sharply, but he ignored the old man and stared at Murong Chui.
“It is the Prince of Wu who refuses to lead us. You command thirty thousand men, yet speak as though a thousand men must starve. You once held armies in your hand. How have you become such a coward?”
Murong Chui rose slowly, making no attempt to evade the blade. Beneath the young man’s armor he saw a patched piece of leather. Its border bore the old pattern used by the Murong army.
“Your father’s?”
Muyu Huan clenched his jaw and nodded.
“I remember that armor. Your father knew better how to hold a knife.”
Footsteps sounded suddenly beyond the hall. Pei Heng and his men reached the entrance with swords half drawn. Murong Chui held up a hand to keep them out.

“Put that away,” he told the young man. “If you mean to kill me today, you can try. But afterward, will you first rescue the people outside the walls, or kill the guards at the granary? With whom will you decide?”
Color came and went in Muyu Huan’s face. His knife dropped a little. Han Yin seized his wrist; the tip struck the table’s corner and shaved away a sliver of wood.

Murong Chui did not take the knife. He returned to the table and studied the map. “Two thousand men on the estates—who commands each band? Where are their weapons kept? By what tally will they pass through the city gates?”
Han Yin’s face tightened. “Are you interrogating us, General?”
“I am giving you one last opportunity to understand what you propose to do.”
Master Feng said, “We are old. There are few left willing to die for Yan. If we do not raise our banner now, our children will no longer know where they came from.”
Wind moved through the hall. The torn edge of the Longcheng map tapped against the wall with a faint papery sound.

Murong Chui rose, went to the old man, and straightened the obsolete bronze cord at his waist. “You taught my brother the Zuo Tradition, sir, and the old stories of the House of Yan. You can still teach them to your grandchildren. But if you mean to teach them rebellion, tell them first how many will die.”
Han Yin asked suddenly, “When you went over to Qin, did you ever imagine returning to Ye one day?”
“I did.”
“This is that night.”
“I have returned,” Murong Chui said softly. “But the Ye I see is not the Ye you see.”

At last he went to the old map. The palace walls of Longcheng stood intact in the picture; not a single street was missing. He reached to touch it, saw how brittle the silk had become, and drew his hand back.

“If you wish to leave, return to your houses and prepare before dawn. Without weapons or troops, you may leave Wei Commandery on county travel permits. I will not stop you. Those who wish to remain may go to the government office tomorrow and give an account of tonight’s discussion. I have already asked where armor is hidden and troops are gathering. The Court of Judicial Review will investigate tomorrow. If anyone attacks a granary or seizes a gate, the garrison will act under military law.”
Muyu Huan sneered. “The Prince of Wu cannot even decide for himself whether to let us go.”
“There are tens of thousands inside and outside these gates. A general’s private promise cannot open the gates on their behalf.”
Han Yin finally looked up. He had hoped Murong Chui would either be provoked into raising a banner or, for old affection’s sake, let an armed band slip out of the city. Both paths were now closed.
“Will Your Highness truly be nothing but Qin’s servant?”
Murong Chui did not answer at once. He lifted the doorway curtain. Damp wind struck his face, carrying the scorched smell of burning wheat stalks.
“I am still Murong Chui.”

He left the hall. Pei Heng walked beside him, noting in his small book the time of entry, the number at the feast, and the appearance of the man with the knife. When he reached Murong Chui’s permission for unarmed former Yan ministers to depart on county documents, his brush paused.
“I must report this exactly as it happened.”
“Do so. And record the private military map kept in the old palace. Make that clear.”
“You are not afraid the court will call you to account?”
“I am. If something happens in the city tomorrow, someone must know what I did tonight.”

Before midnight, Han Yin returned home and spread the map of Longcheng across his main hall. His son asked whether to pack. Han Yin sat beneath the lamp, drew an old silver clasp from his sleeve—a clasp once worn at a Yan palace feast—and set it on the table.
“When I was young, I always thought another royal command would make everything right,” he murmured.
A knock came at the outer gate. A servant sent by Muyu Huan urged them to meet at the eastern gate. Han Yin sat silent for a long time, then ordered the porter to drop the bar.

The western granary caught fire in the third watch. A maidservant feeding the animals at night first saw thick smoke coming from the straw shed behind it. When the gong sounded, refugees thought the authorities were about to cart away all the grain and surged screaming toward the doors. In the darkness someone cried that the Prince of Wu had raised his banner; another shouted that Qin soldiers had burned the stores. Arrows pierced the rain capes of the granary guards.

When Murong Chui arrived, two handcarts had been overturned before the doors. Flames climbed along the timber fence, thin wisps of smoke escaping from the grain sacks. Some urged him to shut the granary and hold it until morning; others wanted to disperse the refugees at once. Instead he ordered the planks nearest the fire torn away, and the untouched grain carried out into the street.

A woman whose hair was soaked rushed forward and clasped a sack. A soldier caught her wrist. Murong Chui ordered him to stop. She said her shelter had had no food for two days. He instructed the granary clerk to enter her name on the spot, allot her one measure according to the shelter’s list, and then asked her to help carry water. She looked at the grain in her arms and actually took up a bucket and ran.

Others gradually followed her to the drainage ditch for water. Pei Heng led cavalry to secure the rear entrance against illicit carts, while the granary clerks marked each sack. Before dawn the fire was out. One timber shed and several hundred measures of grain had burned black, but the western granary remained secure.
News from the eastern gate arrived before the gray smoke had cleared.

Muyu Huan had summoned his estate retainers and attempted to leave the city with bows and armor. They claimed to number three hundred, though fewer than a hundred could actually shoot. They demanded the gate be opened and called upon old Yan military households to join them. When the gate commander refused, Muyu Huan loosed the first arrow, wounding a night guard. The garrison fired back, and the crowd fell into confusion.

By the time Murong Chui rode beneath the walls, the standard-bearer had fallen. The flag hung outside the tower, wet cloth drooping in a single strip. Many of the estate servants knelt in the mud, saying they had thought only that they were setting out on a journey, not attacking a city.
An arrow had struck Muyu Huan in the shoulder, but he still shouted abuse at him. “You promised to let me leave!”
“As one man, or at the head of armed troops? I made myself plain in the hall.”
The young man’s lips moved, but his gaze went to the discarded armor strewn across the ground. The old knife he had brought lay before his knees, a notch broken from its edge.

The gate commander asked for an immediate beheading as a warning. Murong Chui refused. He ordered the wounded man bound and his bleeding stopped, then sent him, with the flag, armor, arrows, and the gate watch register, to the judicial authorities. Pei Heng picked up the banner that had never been fully raised. It was made from the yellow cloth of a grain sack, cut apart and dyed; stitches still showed at one corner.
“To cause all this over such a thing,” Pei Heng said under his breath.
Murong Chui looked at the muddy water running down the banner and gave no answer.

In the afternoon Qin soldiers sealed the old palace. Han Yin came of his own accord to answer questions. The old map still hung behind the place of honor. The lamps were out, and the empty hall smelled of damp earth. Han Yin had not fled; he handed over the list of estate contacts himself. He admitted attending the feast but denied ordering the fire. Murong Chui had Pei Heng seal his statement for examination by the judicial court.
“You will not judge me yourself, General?” Han Yin asked.
“A guard at the eastern gate was struck by an arrow. Guards were wounded at the western granary too. My memories of old days give me no right to pardon those injuries on their behalf.”
Han Yin looked toward the map of Longcheng. “Once I thought you alone refused to turn back. But those who drank with me last night—some left the city, some barred their doors. They all scattered.”

Murong Chui turned. In his youth he, too, had hoped a decree, a flag, a victorious army could draw every heart together. He looked for a long time at the old map, then gave it to Pei Heng to enter in the records and seal away. He ordered soft paper placed beneath the cracked edges of the silk before it was packed.

As he came out of the hall, horns sounded again from the southwest, summoning crews to repair the levee. Murong Chui mounted his horse, the inside of his gloves still stained with ash. Behind him the doors of the old palace closed, leaving Han Yin and a hall of wine from which no one would raise a cup.
“Where are we going?” Pei Heng asked.
“The southern embankment. The river rose during the night.”

They galloped down the long street. The Yan banner that had never been raised was gone from the wall; at the gate soldiers were recording the names of the wounded. Other carts laden with relief grain headed south. Their wheels had stuck in the road, and they waited for someone to lift them out.
